screens.title: Monitoring and Tuning Azure Database for PostgreSQL/MySQL
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn how to approach performance tuning for Azure Database for PostgreSQL and Azure Database for MySQL. We focus on the practical items a database administrator must control: server parameters that shape memory and logging behavior, monitoring signals exposed by Azure Monitor, and the logs that reveal slow queries. You will see concrete examples for PostgreSQL parameters like shared_buffers, work_mem and autovacuum, and MySQL settings like innodb_buffer_pool_size and slow_query_log. We’ll also cover tools that give deeper visibility: pg_stat_statements, SHOW PROCESSLIST, and EXPLAIN. I’ll describe how to enable slow query logging and how to use Azure Diagnostic Settings to send logs to Log Analytics for analysis. Importantly, you will learn common pitfalls such as tuning a buffer too large for available R A M, and why connection pooling can dramatically change observed workload patterns. By the end of the chapter you will be able to change parameters responsibly, collect evidence from metrics and logs, and take the first steps toward targeted query optimization. What tuning step will you try first on your test server?

Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Monitoring and Tuning
Monitoring and Tuning Azure Database for PostgreSQL/MySQL
Configure server parameters, collect metrics and logs, and identify slow queries for targeted optimization.
In this lesson

How to tune server parameters, enable slow query logs, and use Azure Monitor and Log Analytics to find expensive queries.

Why it matters

Managed servers hide infrastructure tasks but require you to tune engine configuration and queries to meet SLAs and control costs.

Starter Key Takeaway

Measure first. Change one parameter at a time, monitor memory and connection metrics, and analyze slow query logs to guide tuning.

Core topics
Server parameters • Monitoring • Slow queries
Server Parameters
Tune memory, buffers and logging levels for PostgreSQL and MySQL via Server parameters blade.
Monitoring
Use Azure Monitor metrics for CPU, memory, IOPS, active connections and replication lag.
Slow Query Analysis
Enable slow query logs and send them to Log Analytics to surface expensive statements.
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
Explore Key Topics
Parameter tuning
Tune shared buffers and buffer pools conservatively and monitor RAM.
Slow query logs
Enable log_min_duration_statement or slow_query_log and ship logs to Log Analytics.
Connection pooling
Use PgBouncer or application pooling to reduce connection overhead and resource spikes.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives focus your practical skills as a DBA working with Azure Database for PostgreSQL and MySQL. First, you will identify and configure the key server parameters that influence memory, buffering and logging. This skill matters because poorly chosen parameters can cause swapping or wasted input and output. Second, you will use Azure Monitor metrics and server logs to observe health and resource usage, allowing you to form an evidence-backed hypothesis before making changes. Third, you will analyze slow query logs and aggregated statement statistics to find queries that deserve indexing or rewriting. Finally, you will understand connection management and how pooling reduces the cost of many short-lived connections. Each objective pairs a specific task with why it matters and a small mnemonic to help you remember the workflow: measure, change, verify, repeat. These are practical, testable skills you will apply in diagnostics and ongoing performance tuning. Consider which objective aligns with your current daily pain point and plan a short experiment to validate a single change.

screens.title: Server Parameters: What they control
screens.narratorSegment: Server parameters are configuration knobs that directly influence how the database engine uses memory, input and output and C P U. For PostgreSQL you will encounter shared_buffers, which reserves memory for caching table data, and work_mem, which controls per-operation memory for sorts and hash joins. autovacuum settings determine how aggressively the engine reclaims space and updates statistics; if autovacuum is too lax, table bloat and degraded planner choices follow. In MySQL, innodb_buffer_pool_size plays the same central caching role for InnoDB data and indexes; an undersized buffer pool forces more physical input and output. You will also see parameters that toggle logging, such as log_min_duration_statement in PostgreSQL or slow_query_log and long_query_time in MySQL. A common misconception is to set buffer sizes to very large values without checking the available R A M; that can cause swapping and worse performance. A safer approach is to choose conservative values, change one parameter at a time, and watch memory and swap metrics after each change. For example, if a server with 8GB R A M has shared_buffers set to 6GB you should monitor total OS memory usage and ensure other processes and connections have headroom. The practical rule is: measure baseline, change one parameter, observe metrics, then iterate. Which parameter will you baseline on your test instance first?

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Server Parameters
Definition
What server parameters control

Parameters control memory allocation, query planning behavior, logging and maintenance tasks that affect throughput and latency.

shared_buffers / innodb_buffer_pool_size
Primary cache for data and indexes. Too large may cause swapping if OS memory is exhausted.
work_mem
Per-operation memory for sorts and hashes; multiplied by concurrent operations, so budget carefully.
autovacuum
Automated background cleanup and stats collection in PostgreSQL to avoid table bloat and stale plans.
Examples & Guidance
Example: For PostgreSQL, a common approach is to set shared_buffers to a fraction of RAM, keep work_mem modest, and tune autovacuum thresholds for large tables. For MySQL, target innodb_buffer_pool_size to hold most frequently accessed data and indexes.
Common Mistake
Tuning in isolation can cause memory pressure. Always view parameters against overall server resources and concurrent workloads.
Key Takeaway
Make single changes, monitor memory and swap metrics, and revert if the change increases paging or errors.
Try This
Record current memory, set a conservative new buffer value, and watch Azure Monitor for memory usage and swap over 24 hours.

screens.title: PostgreSQL Parameters to Know
screens.narratorSegment: Focusing on PostgreSQL, several parameters have outsized impact on performance. shared_buffers controls the server-side cache size for table data; it is not the whole memory story because the OS cache and effective_cache_size also matter. work_mem defines memory used for each sort or hash operation and can multiply across concurrent queries, so a high work_mem helps complex queries but can cause high overall memory use. effective_cache_size gives the planner a hint about how much memory is available for caching, influencing join and index choices. max_connections sets the maximum simultaneous client sessions; too many connections can increase context switching and memory pressure. autovacuum settings determine how frequently vacuum and analyze run; underconfigured autovacuum leads to table bloat and outdated statistics which in turn degrade query plans. A practical example: if you have a reporting workload that runs many large sorts, increasing work_mem for that session or query can improve latency; however, for OLTP with many short transactions, keep work_mem small and control max_connections or use pooling. A misconception to avoid is treating shared_buffers as the only cache—operating system page cache and effective_cache_size must be considered. When you change PostgreSQL settings in Azure, do it through the Server parameters blade and test under representative load.

keyIdea.title: PostgreSQL tuning focus
keyIdea.text: Balance shared_buffers, work_mem and autovacuum based on workload type; use effective_cache_size to guide planner choices.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › PostgreSQL Parameters
Parameters
Key PostgreSQL settings
  • shared_buffers: server cache for table data. Tune to a fraction of RAM and monitor OS usage.
  • work_mem: per-sort/hash memory. Useful to increase for heavy analytic queries but budget by concurrency.
  • effective_cache_size: planner hint about total cache available; influences index vs sequential scan decisions.
  • max_connections: limit to avoid resource exhaustion; use pooling when sessions are numerous.
  • autovacuum: controls automatic cleanup and stats; keep active for large tables to prevent bloat.
Concrete example
A reporting server runs large sorts. Increase work_mem for the reporting role or session, test query runtime and watch total memory. If many reports run concurrently, reduce per-query work_mem and run reports sequentially or on a dedicated replica.
Common Mistake
Raising shared_buffers too close to full RAM without headroom for OS cache and connections can cause swapping—worse than a smaller cache.
Pro Tip
Make statistical changes on a staging server and use representative load tests before applying to production.

screens.title: MySQL Parameters to Know
screens.narratorSegment: In MySQL, and specifically the InnoDB storage engine, innodb_buffer_pool_size is the single most influential parameter for read and write performance. It determines how much memory InnoDB uses to cache data and indexes. When this pool is too small relative to working set size, MySQL performs more physical input and output and C P U waits increase. max_connections controls concurrent sessions and must be set in view of memory per-connection and total available R A M. slow_query_log and long_query_time are logging controls: enable the slow query log and set a long_query_time threshold to capture statements worth investigating. The chapter cautions that query_cache_size is often deprecated or not recommended for high-concurrency workloads. A practical example: if a server with 8GB R A M has innodb_buffer_pool_size of 128MB, as in the provided assessment, the pool is undersized; increasing it to a significant fraction of R A M will reduce input and output. But remember the same caveat: do not exceed physical resources. In Azure managed MySQL some parameters may be restricted; use the Server parameters blade and consult the allowed ranges. When you change logging settings, consider log volume and retention because verbose logs sent to Log Analytics can increase cost and clutter analysis unless filtered carefully.

keyIdea.text: innodb_buffer_pool_size is critical; enable slow_query_log carefully and balance memory allocations with total server resources.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › MySQL Parameters
Key Parameters
MySQL tuning essentials
  • innodb_buffer_pool_size: primary InnoDB cache for data and indexes; set large but within RAM limits.
  • max_connections: limit concurrent sessions to avoid per-connection memory exhaustion.
  • slow_query_log & long_query_time: enable and tune to capture queries over a sensible threshold for your workload.
  • query_cache_size: often deprecated; avoid for high-concurrency workloads where it may cause contention.
Scenario
Admin notices high CPU and slow responses. They inspect innodb buffer settings and find a tiny pool on a server with large RAM. Increasing the pool will likely reduce disk reads and lower CPU wait time. Monitor after change to ensure no swapping.
Watchout
Some parameters are limited by Azure's managed environment. Use the Server parameters blade and check allowed ranges before planning large changes.
Action
Increase innodb_buffer_pool_size to a sensible fraction of RAM and monitor IOPS, read latency, and memory usage.

screens.title: Using Azure Monitor Metrics
screens.narratorSegment: Azure Monitor provides vital metrics to determine if tuning is needed and whether changes are safe. Start by collecting baseline metrics: C P U utilization patterns, memory usage, IOPS and storage throughput, active connections and replication lag for read replicas. These metrics indicate whether a bottleneck is C P U, memory, input and output, or connections. For example, sustained high IOPS and low buffer hit ratio suggest the buffer pool is too small. A spike in active connections alongside high context switching points to connection overload and the need for pooling. The recommended process is: gather baseline metrics during representative workload, identify the dominant resource pressure, form a hypothesis (for example, insufficient innodb buffer), plan a conservative parameter change, apply it in a maintenance window or on a staging replica, and then monitor the same metrics for regression. A common misconception is assuming a single peak equals a chronic problem; verify that peaks are reproducible and align with workload patterns. When you use the Azure portal Metrics blade, build charts that correlate metrics over the same time range so you can see cause and effect. After this cycle you should have evidence-based confidence that a parameter change helped or not.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Azure Monitor Metrics
Process
Measure → Hypothesize → Change → Verify
  1. Collect baseline metrics over representative load periods.
  2. Identify dominant bottleneck: CPU, memory, I/O or connections.
  3. Form a conservative tuning hypothesis (e.g., increase buffer pool).
  4. Apply change on staging or in maintenance window.
  5. Monitor same metrics to confirm improvement or regression.
Supporting Cards
Key metrics
CPU, memory, IOPS, storage throughput, active connections, replication lag.
Correlation
Compare metrics over the same window to see cause and effect rather than isolated numbers.
Example
High disk reads with low buffer hit ratio suggests increasing buffer pool may help rather than adding CPU.
Key Takeaway

Tune based on correlated metrics and validate changes under the same workload to avoid mistaken conclusions.

screens.title: Server Logs and Slow Query Logging
screens.narratorSegment: Server logs are the primary source of truth for query behavior. For PostgreSQL, set log_min_duration_statement to a millisecond threshold to record statements exceeding that duration; for MySQL enable slow_query_log and set long_query_time. Enabling these logs lets you capture slow individual statements, but remember that logs can be noisy. Send logs to Log Analytics via Diagnostic Settings so you can query them with KQL and correlate them with metrics. A concrete example: set log_min_duration_statement to 500 to capture queries taking longer than half a second. After enabling, run representative workloads and confirm logs appear in your Log Analytics workspace. A common misconception is relying only on slow query logs to find the worst offenders. Slow query logs capture long-running statements but miss frequently called statements that are moderately slow; use pg_stat_statements to find cumulative cost. Also be careful with log verbosity in production, since very low thresholds or enabling log_statement = 'all' can quickly produce large volumes. Plan retention and filter at ingestion if necessary. In short, slow query logging is essential but part of a larger diagnostics pipeline that includes aggregated statistics and execution plans.

keyIdea.text: Enable slow query logging to collect slow statements, ship logs to Log Analytics, and balance threshold and verbosity to avoid noise.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Server Logs
How to enable
PostgreSQL and MySQL logging
  • PostgreSQL: set log_min_duration_statement to a threshold like 500 to log queries slower than 500ms.
  • MySQL: set slow_query_log = ON and long_query_time = 1 to capture queries over one second.
  • Use Diagnostic Settings to send PostgreSQLLogs or MySQL logs to a Log Analytics workspace for analysis.
Best practices
Choose thresholds that balance usefulness against log volume. Test threshold values in staging, and ensure retention and filtering are configured to keep costs manageable.
Example
Set log_min_duration_statement = 500, run a report, wait for logs to arrive in Log Analytics, then filter by duration to find slow statements.
Misconception
Logs alone don't reveal frequency or cumulative cost. Combine logs with aggregated stats to prioritize optimizations.

screens.title: Analyzing Slow Queries in Log Analytics (KQL)
screens.narratorSegment: Once your database logs flow into Log Analytics, you can run Kusto queries to extract slow statements and inspect their duration and context. A typical KQL pattern filters the AzureDiagnostics table for the resource provider for your server, matches the logs category for PostgreSQL or MySQL logs, parses out a duration field from the message, and then selects records above your threshold. For example, you will search for messages that include the text 'duration:' and project the parsed duration and the statement text, ordering by time to find the most recent slow executions. An important practical point is to wait a few minutes for logs to propagate and to use time range filters to narrow your search. A common mistake is looking only at the most recent slow single query; instead, inspect frequency and identify whether the same query signature appears repeatedly. After you find candidate queries, copy the text and run EXPLAIN in a safe environment or use pg_stat_statements to see aggregated impact. This workflow gives you a repeatable way to move from raw logs to prioritized optimization actions. Which KQL filter will you try first on your workspace?

keyIdea.title: From logs to action
keyIdea.text: Use KQL to parse durations and query text from database logs, then prioritize statements by frequency and total cost.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › KQL for Slow Queries
KQL Example
AzureDiagnostics
| where ResourceProvider == "MICROSOFT.DBFORPOSTGRESQL"
| where Category == "PostgreSQLLogs"
| parse Message with * "duration: " duration_ms:long " ms  statement: " query_text:string
| where isnotempty(duration_ms) and duration_ms > 500
| project TimeGenerated, Resource, query_text, duration_ms
| order by TimeGenerated desc
Explanation
  • Filter logs for your provider and category to narrow to database logs.
  • Parse the message to extract duration and the statement text for easy sorting.
  • Order by time and duration to find recent and long-running statements for inspection.
Pro Tip

Use time filters and grouping to find frequently occurring statements rather than only the single slowest execution.

screens.title: Using pg_stat_statements
screens.narratorSegment: pg_stat_statements aggregates execution statistics across all statements and is invaluable for finding statements that cost the most cumulatively. To use it in Azure Database for PostgreSQL you must enable shared_preload_libraries to include pg_stat_statements, and set tracking parameters such as pg_stat_statements. track and pg_stat_statements. max in Server parameters, then restart if required. After it collects data, you can query the view to see total_time, calls, mean_time and hit ratio. A practical pattern is to order by total_time descending and inspect the top queries; these may be frequently-run lightweight queries or infrequent heavy ones. A common misconception is that only the slowest single queries matter; pg_stat_statements reveals moderate queries that run often and add up to significant cost. Use the aggregated data to prioritize index creation, query rewriting, or caching. Remember to limit the extension's settings to an appropriate memory footprint for your server. After you identify candidates, run EXPLAIN to understand execution plans before making structural changes. Using pg_stat_statements means pg_stat_statements shows cumulative cost to prioritize queries that consume the most total resources, not just the slowest single runs.. In practical terms, enable the extension and query aggregated statement statistics to find high cumulative cost queries. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

narration.text: pg_stat_statements aggregates execution statistics across all statements and is invaluable for finding statements that cost the most cumulatively. content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › pg_stat_statements
Enable & Query
-- Server parameters to set in Azure portal:
shared_preload_libraries = 'pg_stat_statements'
pg_stat_statements.track = 'all'
pg_stat_statements.max = 10000
pg_stat_statements.track_utility = off

-- After restart, query aggregated stats:
SELECT
  query,
  calls,
  total_time,
  mean_time,
  rows,
  100.0 * shared_blks_hit / (shared_blks_hit + shared_blks_read + 1) AS hit_ratio
FROM pg_stat_statements
ORDER BY total_time DESC
LIMIT 10;
How to use results
  • Sort by total_time to find aggregated cost and prioritize optimizations.
  • Check calls multiplied by mean_time to spot high-frequency, moderate-cost queries.
  • Combine with EXPLAIN to understand whether indexes or rewrites will help.
Key Takeaway

pg_stat_statements complements slow logs by surfacing cumulative cost across all executions, essential for prioritization.

screens.title: EXPLAIN: Reading Execution Plans
screens.narratorSegment: EXPLAIN shows the query execution plan and is essential before making schema or index changes. In both PostgreSQL and MySQL you'll use EXPLAIN to reveal whether a query uses an index, performs sequential scans, or executes expensive sorts and nested loops. The first step is to capture the slow or high-cost query text from logs or pg_stat_statements. Then run EXPLAIN or EXPLAIN ANALYZE in a safe environment to see estimated and actual row counts. Look for large sequential scans on wide tables or nested loops that process many rows due to missing join indexes. A concrete example: a filter on value_col without an index results in a sequential scan; adding an index on value_col can turn that into an index scan and dramatically reduce input and output. A common misconception is assuming EXPLAIN's estimated costs are absolute; they are estimates based on statistics, so ensure table statistics are recent. Use ANALYZE or a recent autovacuum run to refresh stats before making final decisions. EXPLAIN guides you from symptom to targeted structural fixes like indexes or query rewrites. EXPLAIN: Reading Execution Plans means use explain to diagnose plan shapes and confirm whether indexes or rewrites will reduce i/o and cpu.. In practical terms, use explain to understand how queries access data and where to add indexes or rewrite joins. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. EXPLAIN Example
-- MySQL example
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM large_table WHERE value_col = 50000;

-- PostgreSQL example
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM large_table WHERE value_col = 50000;
Reading the plan
  • Look for Seq Scan or full table scan on large tables—this signals missing indexes.
  • Check nested loop and sort operations that process many rows; consider different join orders or indexes.
  • Refresh statistics with ANALYZE before heavy decisions to ensure estimates are accurate.
Misconception

Estimated cost numbers are helpful but not absolute—use actual timings and row counts from ANALYZE to guide fixes.

screens.title: Connection Management and Pooling
screens.narratorSegment: Connection management matters because each open session consumes memory and can add scheduling overhead on the server. In many applications, opening a new connection per request causes high connection churn and resource pressure. Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server includes built-in PgBouncer support, while Single Server or MySQL often require application-level pooling or a proxy such as ProxySQL. Connection pooling works by maintaining a pool of established backend connections that are reused by application requests, reducing the cost of connection establishment and lowering average active connections at the database. A practical scenario: a web tier with 1000 short requests per second can overwhelm the server if each request opens a fresh connection; pooling with a small number of persistent connections dramatically stabilizes server memory use and reduces context switching. A common mistake is increasing max_connections to a very high value as a quick fix—without sufficient R A M, this can cause out-of-memory. The correct flow is to cap database connections, implement pooling, and measure active connections via Azure Monitor. Ask yourself: does my workload need persistent connections or a pooled model to stabilize resource usage?

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Connection Pooling
Why it matters
Reduce overhead, prevent spikes

Pooling keeps a bounded set of active database connections and reuses them for many application requests, lowering memory and connection spikes on the server.

Built-in / external
Flexible Server: PgBouncer may be available. Single Server / MySQL: use ProxySQL or application pooling libraries.
Key Takeaway
Prefer pooling over increasing max_connections; monitor Active Connections to validate capacity.
Scenario Card
A bursty API opened thousands of short connections and caused resource exhaustion. Implementing a connection pool limited backend sessions and reduced memory usage and connection errors.
Common Mistake
Raising max_connections without changing workload or adding memory is often a temporary fix that leads to swapping or crashes.

screens.title: A Practical Tuning Workflow and Common Mistakes
screens.narratorSegment: Successful tuning follows a disciplined workflow. Begin by recording a baseline of key metrics: C P U, memory, IOPS, active connections and storage latency during representative workloads. Next, collect evidence from logs—enable slow query logging and send logs to Log Analytics or enable pg_stat_statements for aggregated statistics. Analyze logs to identify candidates for optimization, and use EXPLAIN to inspect execution plans for those queries. Formulate a single change: a parameter tweak, an index addition, or a query rewrite. Apply the change on a staging replica or during a maintenance window, and monitor the same baseline metrics for regressions. If the change helps, roll forward and continue iterating; if not, revert and try a different approach. Common mistakes to avoid: changing multiple parameters at once (which prevents causality analysis), increasing buffer sizes beyond physical R A M, and assuming the slowest single query is the highest priority. A concrete example: identify a frequent medium-cost query via pg_stat_statements, run EXPLAIN, add a covering index, and measure latency and IOPS improvement. This repeatable cycle reduces risk and builds confidence over time. A Practical Tuning Workflow and Common Mistakes means baseline → collect logs → analyze → change one thing → validate → iterate; avoid simultaneous changes and monitor resources closely.. In practical terms, step-by-step process to tune safely and avoid pitfalls like tuning in isolation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Tuning Workflow
Step-by-step
  1. Record baseline metrics under representative load.
  2. Enable and collect slow logs; enable pg_stat_statements if possible.
  3. Prioritize queries by frequency and cumulative time, not only single slow runs.
  4. Use EXPLAIN to inspect plans and decide index or rewrite strategies.
  5. Apply one change, monitor same metrics, and iterate.

  • Targeting only single slow executions and ignoring high-frequency moderate-cost queries.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn how to approach performance tuning for Azure Database for PostgreSQL and Azure Database for MySQL. We focus on the practical items a database administrator must control: server parameters that shape memory and logging behavior, monitoring signals exposed by Azure Monitor, and the logs that reveal slow queries. You will see concrete examples for PostgreSQL parameters like shared_buffers, work_mem and autovacuum, and MySQL settings like innodb_buffer_pool_size and slow_query_log. We’ll also cover tools that give deeper visibility: pg_stat_statements, SHOW PROCESSLIST, and EXPLAIN. I’ll describe how to enable slow query logging and how to use Azure Diagnostic Settings to send logs to Log Analytics for analysis. Importantly, you will learn common pitfalls such as tuning a buffer too large for available R A M, and why connection pooling can dramatically change observed workload patterns. By the end of the chapter you will be able to change parameters responsibly, collect evidence from metrics and logs, and take the first steps toward targeted query optimization. What tuning step will you try first on your test server?

These objectives focus your practical skills as a DBA working with Azure Database for PostgreSQL and MySQL. First, you will identify and configure the key server parameters that influence memory, buffering and logging. This skill matters because poorly chosen parameters can cause swapping or wasted input and output. Second, you will use Azure Monitor metrics and server logs to observe health and resource usage, allowing you to form an evidence-backed hypothesis before making changes. Third, you will analyze slow query logs and aggregated statement statistics to find queries that deserve indexing or rewriting. Finally, you will understand connection management and how pooling reduces the cost of many short-lived connections. Each objective pairs a specific task with why it matters and a small mnemonic to help you remember the workflow: measure, change, verify, repeat. These are practical, testable skills you will apply in diagnostics and ongoing performance tuning. Consider which objective aligns with your current daily pain point and plan a short experiment to validate a single change.

These additional objectives emphasize the tools and commands that let you perform deep analysis. You will enable and query pg_stat_statements to aggregate execution statistics and find statements that consume the most cumulative time. You will run SHOW PROCESSLIST in MySQL to inspect current queries and states, and use EXPLAIN in both engines to read execution plans. You will also learn to configure Diagnostic Settings so database logs flow into Log Analytics, where KQL helps you filter slow statements. Each objective links a command or tool to a practical outcome: find frequent slow callers, see blocking or long-running sessions, and discover missing indexes or suboptimal plans. A common misconception is that the slowest single query is always the top target; instead, you will learn to balance frequency and cost. These techniques help you prioritize optimizations that reduce overall load rather than only trimming the single slowest statement.

Server parameters are configuration knobs that directly influence how the database engine uses memory, input and output and C P U. For PostgreSQL you will encounter shared_buffers, which reserves memory for caching table data, and work_mem, which controls per-operation memory for sorts and hash joins. autovacuum settings determine how aggressively the engine reclaims space and updates statistics; if autovacuum is too lax, table bloat and degraded planner choices follow. In MySQL, innodb_buffer_pool_size plays the same central caching role for InnoDB data and indexes; an undersized buffer pool forces more physical input and output. You will also see parameters that toggle logging, such as log_min_duration_statement in PostgreSQL or slow_query_log and long_query_time in MySQL. A common misconception is to set buffer sizes to very large values without checking the available R A M; that can cause swapping and worse performance. A safer approach is to choose conservative values, change one parameter at a time, and watch memory and swap metrics after each change. For example, if a server with 8GB R A M has shared_buffers set to 6GB you should monitor total OS memory usage and ensure other processes and connections have headroom. The practical rule is: measure baseline, change one parameter, observe metrics, then iterate. Which parameter will you baseline on your test instance first?

Focusing on PostgreSQL, several parameters have outsized impact on performance. shared_buffers controls the server-side cache size for table data; it is not the whole memory story because the OS cache and effective_cache_size also matter. work_mem defines memory used for each sort or hash operation and can multiply across concurrent queries, so a high work_mem helps complex queries but can cause high overall memory use. effective_cache_size gives the planner a hint about how much memory is available for caching, influencing join and index choices. max_connections sets the maximum simultaneous client sessions; too many connections can increase context switching and memory pressure. autovacuum settings determine how frequently vacuum and analyze run; underconfigured autovacuum leads to table bloat and outdated statistics which in turn degrade query plans. A practical example: if you have a reporting workload that runs many large sorts, increasing work_mem for that session or query can improve latency; however, for OLTP with many short transactions, keep work_mem small and control max_connections or use pooling. A misconception to avoid is treating shared_buffers as the only cache—operating system page cache and effective_cache_size must be considered. When you change PostgreSQL settings in Azure, do it through the Server parameters blade and test under representative load.

In MySQL, and specifically the InnoDB storage engine, innodb_buffer_pool_size is the single most influential parameter for read and write performance. It determines how much memory InnoDB uses to cache data and indexes. When this pool is too small relative to working set size, MySQL performs more physical input and output and C P U waits increase. max_connections controls concurrent sessions and must be set in view of memory per-connection and total available R A M. slow_query_log and long_query_time are logging controls: enable the slow query log and set a long_query_time threshold to capture statements worth investigating. The chapter cautions that query_cache_size is often deprecated or not recommended for high-concurrency workloads. A practical example: if a server with 8GB R A M has innodb_buffer_pool_size of 128MB, as in the provided assessment, the pool is undersized; increasing it to a significant fraction of R A M will reduce input and output. But remember the same caveat: do not exceed physical resources. In Azure managed MySQL some parameters may be restricted; use the Server parameters blade and consult the allowed ranges. When you change logging settings, consider log volume and retention because verbose logs sent to Log Analytics can increase cost and clutter analysis unless filtered carefully.

Azure Monitor provides vital metrics to determine if tuning is needed and whether changes are safe. Start by collecting baseline metrics: C P U utilization patterns, memory usage, IOPS and storage throughput, active connections and replication lag for read replicas. These metrics indicate whether a bottleneck is C P U, memory, input and output, or connections. For example, sustained high IOPS and low buffer hit ratio suggest the buffer pool is too small. A spike in active connections alongside high context switching points to connection overload and the need for pooling. The recommended process is: gather baseline metrics during representative workload, identify the dominant resource pressure, form a hypothesis (for example, insufficient innodb buffer), plan a conservative parameter change, apply it in a maintenance window or on a staging replica, and then monitor the same metrics for regression. A common misconception is assuming a single peak equals a chronic problem; verify that peaks are reproducible and align with workload patterns. When you use the Azure portal Metrics blade, build charts that correlate metrics over the same time range so you can see cause and effect. After this cycle you should have evidence-based confidence that a parameter change helped or not.

Server logs are the primary source of truth for query behavior. For PostgreSQL, set log_min_duration_statement to a millisecond threshold to record statements exceeding that duration; for MySQL enable slow_query_log and set long_query_time. Enabling these logs lets you capture slow individual statements, but remember that logs can be noisy. Send logs to Log Analytics via Diagnostic Settings so you can query them with KQL and correlate them with metrics. A concrete example: set log_min_duration_statement to 500 to capture queries taking longer than half a second. In short, slow query logging is essential but part of a larger diagnostics pipeline that includes aggregated statistics and execution plans.

A typical KQL pattern filters the AzureDiagnostics table for the resource provider for your server, matches the logs category for PostgreSQL or MySQL logs, parses out a duration field from the message, and then selects records above your threshold. A practical scenario: a web tier with 1000 short requests per second can overwhelm the server if each request opens a fresh connection; pooling with a small number of persistent connections dramatically stabilizes server memory use and reduces context switching. A common mistake is increasing max_connections to a very high value as a quick fix—without sufficient R A M, this can cause out-of-memory. The correct flow is to cap database connections, implement pooling, and measure active connections via Azure Monitor. Ask yourself: does my workload need persistent connections or a pooled model to stabilize resource usage?

Successful tuning follows a disciplined workflow. Begin by recording a baseline of key metrics: C P U, memory, IOPS, active connections and storage latency during representative workloads. Next, collect evidence from logs—enable slow query logging and send logs to Log Analytics or enable pg_stat_statements for aggregated statistics. Analyze logs to identify candidates for optimization, and use EXPLAIN to inspect execution plans for those queries. Formulate a single change: a parameter tweak, an index addition, or a query rewrite. Apply the change on a staging replica or during a maintenance window, and monitor the same baseline metrics for regressions. If the change helps, roll forward and continue iterating; if not, revert and try a different approach. Common mistakes to avoid: changing multiple parameters at once (which prevents causality analysis), increasing buffer sizes beyond physical R A M, and assuming the slowest single query is the highest priority. A concrete example: identify a frequent medium-cost query via pg_stat_statements, run EXPLAIN, add a covering index, and measure latency and IOPS improvement. This repeatable cycle reduces risk and builds confidence over time. Keep four concepts in mind as you tune Azure Database for PostgreSQL and MySQL. First, server parameters control critical resource allocation—set them conservatively and validate changes. Second, slow query logs are invaluable for finding long-running statements, but combine them with aggregated statistics to find high cumulative cost queries. Third, use EXPLAIN and pg_stat_statements to inspect plans and prioritize optimizations instead of guessing. Fourth, connection pooling stabilizes resource usage and is often preferable to raising max_connections. Together, these ideas form a practical workflow: measure, collect logs, analyze, change one thing, and verify.
